welcome.subject: You're in
welcome.body:
{handle}, your invite to the Backroom went through. That is where the work is posted and where it is paid.

Open the Route map, pick The Backroom in your address book and connect. Log in with your invite and look at Contracts. Take the library job first. It is small, and nobody there is watching or tracing anything. I will point at what to press.

If you want the whole desk explained first, the tour is in the menu (the button with three lines). You do not need it for this.

I vouched for you. Don't make me regret it.

Wren

firstAccept.subject: How a job goes
firstAccept.body:
Good. Every job runs the same way.

One. Disconnect from the Backroom. Your gateway holds one connection at a time.

Two. On the Route map, add a relay or two before you connect to the target. Every relay is one more step a trace has to follow, which is time for you. Spread them across the world: a trace crawls across oceans and races through hops inside one country.

Three. Connect, break the administrator password, log in and do what the contract says. Your contract, at the top right, shows when it is done.

Four. Open Logs, scrub the lines that show you, then disconnect. Lines left behind get you fined.

If the trace warning turns red, the number is how long you have. Leave early if you must and go back in.

When it is done, press your contract and then Deliver. You are paid on the spot.

Wren

firstDelivery.subject: First one done
firstDelivery.body:
That is a first job delivered. The library was the easy one: nobody there ever traces anyone. Everywhere else somebody does. The next target is slow about it, so use it to learn. Put a relay or two on the route before you connect. The Route map tells you how long they need.

Some systems put a proxy or a firewall in your way. A proxy stops you changing records and logs. A firewall stops you copying and deleting files. The Market sells a bypass for each. Buy them when a job needs them, not before.

While a firewall bypass runs you can line up its ports by hand, which is much faster. And if a trace is closing in, reroute through a spare server on the Route map. That makes the trace start that step again.

Wren

paid.subject: Paid: {title}
paid.body:
Received. {pay} credits have been sent to your account through the Backroom.

We will not speak again.

contractFailed.subject: Contract withdrawn: {title}
contractFailed.body:
I hear {target} traced someone last night. I cannot be connected to that.

The contract is withdrawn. If it appears on the board again, it will be because I had no better option.

caught.subject: Heard you got traced
caught.body:
{target} followed you home. Word gets around.

They have fined you {fine} credits and changed their passwords, so whatever you had broken there is gone. For {hours} hours the Backroom will only offer you standing work, and it pays less. Lie low, take the small jobs or let the clock run, and come back.

Next time use more relays, and leave before the timer says you have to.

Wren

review.subject: They read their logs
review.body:
{target} went through its access log after you left and found {lines} that should not have been there. It was enough to put a name to.

They have fined you {fine} credits. No trace this time, so the Backroom still has work for you.

Before you disconnect, open Logs and scrub your login and anything that says a file was copied, deleted or a record changed. The lines that only say a connection opened or closed prove nothing.

Wren

harderSecurity.subject: Harder doors
harderSecurity.body:
{handle}, the board will start showing you jobs with better locks on them. Two things you have not met.

Some monitors start tracing the moment you connect. The Market now sells a Monitor Bypass. Run it from the security strip before you log in. While the monitor is blind, nothing you do is noticed and a running trace stands still. When it comes back it sees you if you are still an administrator or a program is still running. So it buys a head start, not a free pass, and it works once per connection. When it lands you are shown the monitor's check-in pattern. Repeat it to stay hidden longer.

Some files are encrypted. You can copy one but not read it, and no client pays for it until it is open. Buy the Decrypter and run it from Programs, on your own gateway. It keeps working after you disconnect.

Wren

phishing.subject: People are the soft part
phishing.body:
{handle}, breaking a password is slow and loud. Asking for it is neither.

When you are on a server, read the files. Your gateway keeps a note of every person a file names and every detail worth repeating.

Then open Messages and press Write to someone. Each lead is something a person you have found could give you. Pick one, pick whose name goes on the message (somebody that person would do this for), and pick up to three details that name would know. The right name with the right details gets an answer in under an hour.

Get it wrong and they go quiet for a few hours. Get it wrong twice and they report it, their side changes its passwords, and the board hears about it.

Start at the Open Relay Registry. Its public files say more than they should about the people at Polar Mesh.

Wren

phishRefused.subject: Re: {label}

phishReported.subject: You were reported
phishReported.body:
{name} did not believe your second message either, and this time they passed it up the line.

Their side has changed its passwords, so anything you had broken there is gone, and {name} will not answer you again. The board has heard, and your rating has taken the knock.

Read more before you write. The details have to be ones that person would know.

Wren

models.subject: Hire some help
models.body:
{handle}, you are doing enough work now that some of it is not worth your own time.

The Backroom's Market rents language models by the day, from a compute farm that does not ask what they are for. A model lives on their hardware and works through your gateway.

Magpie is small and cheap. Log in somewhere, open Files, and it will read every file there in one go and note the people and details for you. In Logs it will pick out the lines that point at you.

Kestrel only watches. If a trace is about to reach you, Kestrel cuts the line first. You lose the connection, not the fine.

Heron is large and costs three times what Magpie does. It does both jobs, and it will also read a message over before you send it and tell you if the name or the details are wrong.

A rental lasts a day. Rent one when you have a day's work lined up.

Wren

modelExpired.subject: Your rental has ended: {model}
modelExpired.body:
Your day with {model} is over and the instance has been wiped. Nothing it read has been kept on our side.

Rent it again from the Market on your board whenever you like.

Lowlight Compute
No logs. No questions. No refunds.

hardware.subject: Your gateway is slow
hardware.body:
{handle}, you are still on the machine you started with. It shows.

The Backroom has a Hardware shelf now, next to the Market. A faster processor runs every program quicker and runs more of them at once. More storage holds more of what you bring home. A better modem moves files faster, so the firewall is open for less time. A second port lets you hold two connections at once, and some jobs need that.

If you are tired of paying Lowlight by the day, there is an inference card that runs a model on your own gateway for good.

Parts install the moment you pay. Nobody buys them back.

One warning. The big systems do not just fine you when they trace you. They push something back down the line, and you lose a part. Be careful where you get caught.

hardwareLost.subject: They burned a part
hardwareLost.body:
That trace did more than find you. Whoever runs that system pushed something back down the line, and your {part} did not survive it.

Your gateway is running on {now} in that slot until you replace it. The Hardware shelf at the Backroom has what you need, if you have the credits.

jobs.subject: Between the real jobs
jobs.body:
{handle}, the board has more than the named jobs now. Look for the ones against ordinary companies. Nobody special is behind them, they are just work: copy a file, delete one, change a record. They come and go, and a new batch appears every day or two.

Three things to know. The harder your name, the harder the companies it posts against, and the better they pay. The real contracts make your name faster, but each one waits until your rating is high enough for the client to trust you with it. The board tells you what rating the next one wants. Standing work is how you get there.

Wren

links.subject: Two doors at once
links.body:
{handle}, a word about the better-defended systems. The best ones are not defended by the company that owns them. A security firm runs their firewall, or a desk in another building watches their monitor, and each of those has a login of its own.

If you hold an administrator session on that other machine, the layer it guards switches off while you are there. Close the session and it comes back on.

You will need a gateway that holds two connections at once. Read what is on the small servers before you go for the big ones. Their handover notes say a lot.

Wren

skills.subject: Habits
skills.body:
{handle}, you have been at this long enough to have habits, and habits are worth choosing.

Every three steps up the board earns a skill point, counted from your best name ever, so getting traced never takes one back. Open Skills and spend them on three paths. Intrusion is for getting in: faster breakers, a steadier hand on a port line-up. Ghost is for not being found: slower traces, monitors that give you longer. Engineering is for building rather than buying: a quicker gateway, smaller builds, taking other people's tools apart.

Nobody does all three well. If you pick wrong, the Backroom will help you forget, for a fee that goes up each time.

Wren

workbench.subject: Something for your bench
workbench.body:
{handle}, everyone buys the same programs from the same market, so every monitor in the city knows what they look like.

I have put two modules on your gateway, a Swift and a Quiet. Open Programs and go to its Workbench tab. Pick a program you own, fit a module and build. Your original stays as it was, and you choose which one runs. Scrap a build and you get its modules back.

Four kinds. Swift is faster and a little bigger. Compact is much smaller and slightly slower. Quiet paces its traffic like ordinary use, so a monitor looks past it. Tidy leaves no log line behind. Each comes in three grades.

Builds take time and room on your drive. More modules are on the Backroom Market, and some servers leave .mod installers lying about: copy one and the module is yours. Some clients pay in modules, so read the briefs.

Wren

decompiling.subject: Taking tools apart
decompiling.body:
{handle}, that file you copied home is not data. It is a compiled program, the kind that ends in .bin. Some systems keep their own tools on the server, and every one of them is built from the same parts you fit at the Workbench.

The Backroom's Market sells a Decompiler. Run it on the file from Programs, on your own gateway, like the Decrypter. It takes a while, and it uses the file up. What comes out is the modules it was built from, added to your parts. Now and then the file turns out to be a copy of something the Market sells, and then you get that program as well, for nothing.

There is a skill for this too. Teardown, under Engineering, gets one more module out of every file you take apart.

Wren

routes.subject: Relays are not what they were
routes.body:
{handle}, the easy years are over. Three things about routes have changed.

Relays warm up. Every connection through a server leaves it warmer, and a warm relay holds a trace up for less time. They cool over a few hours, so rotate them. The address book marks the warm ones.

A good monitor sees through a poor relay. Pick your target first and the map will tell you which relays it sees through. Every company you break into is worth keeping as a relay.

A trace gathers pace. The first three steps back from the target take their full time, and each one after that takes less. Put your best relays last, next to the target.

The Backroom sells a Route Planner that fills a route in one press. You can also keep three routes of your own on the map.

Wren

stages.subject: Jobs with more than one step
stages.body:
{handle}, some jobs on the board run to several steps now. You will take one, do the first part, and the client will write again with the next: a file to find before you can reach the real target, a key to lift from one server to open another, maybe a choice at the end about who you sell to.

Your contract, at the top right of the screen, shows every step and which one you are on. The next target's address comes with each new step, so watch your inbox. Pay climbs with the length, and so does the heat, so plan the whole chain before you start, not one server at a time.

contractLate.subject: Too slow: {title}
contractLate.body: You missed the window on this one, {handle}. The moment has passed and the job is off. No payment. These things keep, so be ready next time.

defence.subject: You have a name now
defence.body:
{handle}, you are known well enough now that someone may come looking, and not to hire you. After a noisy job, someone may try your gateway while you are off the wire.

When it happens, the Defence window opens on its own. The intruder works through your layers one barrier at a time, and you have four answers. Close the port they are probing, a line-up that sets them back. Trace them back for their address, and if you finish first their server is yours to raid. Lock a file or two you would hate to lose. Or pull the plug, which always works but tells you nothing.

Lose and they take credits, wipe a file, or leave a trail that brings a log review. They cannot touch your hardware or end your career.

Wren

raid.subject: INTRUSION ON YOUR GATEWAY
raid.body:
Someone is on your gateway. The handle on the session reads {who}. If they get in, they will {style}.

Open Defence on your bar. Close their ports to slow them, trace them back for their address, lock what you cannot lose, or pull the plug.

raidWon.subject: Traced: {who}
raidWon.body:
You ran the trace home before they got in. {who} was coming from {home}, at {address}. It is in your address book now, and whatever they left lying there is yours for the taking.

They will not try you again in a hurry.

raidLost.subject: They got in: {who}
raidLost.body:
{who} broke through before you could stop them and {loss}.

"{taunt}"

No hardware lost, and you are still in business. Next time, trace them.

raidFled.subject: Plug pulled
raidFled.body: You pulled the plug on {who}. Every connection dropped and your gateway went dark. They got nothing, and nor did you: no address, no loot. Sometimes that is the right call.

shops.subject: The Backroom is not the only shelf
shops.body:
{handle}, you have been buying everything from one counter. It is not the only one.

The Open Relay Registry lists three more shops. Tin Shed sells programs and modules, including odd ones that are quick but fat, or slow but small. Varga Surplus sells gateway hardware a little under the Backroom's price. Lowtide Exchange sells specialist kit and costs a quarter more. Its daily lines are the things that should not be for sale, and they change at midnight.

None of them post work. Log in as a walk-in and look around.

Two programs of the same kind and version are not the same program. Read the sizes and the times. Whichever is loaded in memory is the one that runs.

Wren

gear.subject: Things that are not locks
gear.body:
{handle}, the work you are getting now is not only about getting through the door. Four things that help with everything else.

A Scanner reads a server's security before you connect, so you buy the right bypass first and not the wrong one. A Trace Jammer freezes a trace for a few seconds, once on each connection. It is not a way out. It is a way to finish. A trace sensor, a part for your gateway, reads a trace to the second without a Tracker program taking up room. And a module called Offload lets a program you build run off to the side, without using one of your slots.

None of them make you quiet. All of them make you a little less loud.

Wren

news.subject: You made the paper
news.body:
{handle}, have a look at the Wire this morning. {company} is on the front page.

They don't know who you are and they never will, if you keep doing it properly. But they know someone was there, and a company that has just been hit puts its guard up for a few days. One that gets hit three times hires a firm, and then it stays hard. The map marks the ones on their guard.

Read the paper now and then. It isn't only about you. Outages, layoffs, auditors: when something goes wrong at a company, somebody always wants a job done there while the door is open. Those jobs go up on the board, and they don't stay long.

Wren

memory.subject: What you carry
memory.body:
{handle}, a word about your gateway before it catches you out.

It has a drive and it has memory. The drive keeps everything you own. Memory is smaller, and only what is loaded there can run on someone else's server. One program of each kind, and once you are inside, what you brought is what you have.

Open Programs on your bar. The strip at the top is your memory. Click a program to load it or send it back to the drive, and keep up to three loadouts for the kinds of work you do. A steal needs a copier and no deleter. A wipe is the other way round. If the place has a proxy and you mean to clean the log, bring the bypass.

A Scanner tells you what a server has before you connect, which tells you what to pack. More memory is on the Hardware shelf. Smaller tools come off your Workbench.

Wren

property.subject: Three addresses
property.body:
{handle}, we have not met. I place things for people who cannot put their own name on a lease, and yours has started to come up.

I keep three on my books that would suit you. A rack in a harbour hall in Reykjavik, to route through: nobody else is on it, so it never warms up. A second address in Porto, for the day a trace gets home: it finds that door and not yours. And room in Tallinn for a second rig beside your first.

None of it is cheap, and I sell to names I know, so the last two will wait until yours is bigger. You will find me on the Hardware shelf of any board that sells parts, under Property.

I. Maran

legend.subject: What is left
legend.body:
{handle}, there is no title above the one you have. I checked.

What there is now is a different kind of offer. Once a day the board will carry one marked Legend: two steps, against the hardest places there are, at three times the money. Each comes with a condition, and the condition changes with the week. A short fuse. Every lock a level up. No room to carry much. No reading on the trace. It holds only while that job is open, and the board says which before you take it.

Nobody needs you to do them. That is rather the point.

Wren
